title: Retirement of a Partner
outcomes: Work out the new ratio and the gaining ratio of the continuing partners in every standard situation.
Record revaluation, reserves and goodwill on retirement and close the retiring partner's capital account.
Settle the retiring partner's claim in cash, as a loan, or in instalments with interest, and prepare the loan account.
Account for joint life policies under all three methods and for separate life policies on retirement.

meta.exam_tip: In a retirement question the retiring partner's capital column must end at nil — paid in cash or transferred to loan. If it does not close, something has been missed.

concepts.title: Retirement: the firm continues, one partner leaves
body: A partner may retire because of age, health, a new career or a dispute. The firm does not close: the remaining (continuing) partners carry on the business, so it is a reconstitution.

The continuing partners take over the retiring partner's share of future profits — they gain. In return, they must settle everything that is due to him: his capital, his share of reserves and undistributed profits, his share of revaluation profit (or loss), his share of goodwill, and his share of any joint life policy.

Steps: (1) new ratio and gaining ratio, (2) revaluation, (3) reserves, (4) goodwill, (5) life policy, (6) find the final balance of the retiring partner and settle it — in cash, as a loan, or in instalments.
concepts.analogy: A flatmate moving out: the others take over her room, and in exchange they refund her deposit and her share of everything bought together.
concepts.work: A retirement settlement statement is one of the most sensitive documents an accountant prepares — the retiring partner (often with his own adviser) checks every line before signing the release deed.

concepts.title: Gaining ratio and the new ratio
body: Gain of a continuing partner = new share − old share. The ratio of these gains is the gaining (benefit) ratio. It is used to debit the continuing partners with the retiring partner's share of goodwill.
If nothing is said, the continuing partners share in their old ratio — strike out the retiring partner's figure — and the gaining ratio is their old ratio.
If the new ratio is given, compute gains = new − old for each. If the gains (the parts of the retiring partner's share each one takes) are given, new share = old share + gain.
concepts.analogy: When one player leaves a relay team, the others run his leg; who runs how much of it decides who "gained" his lap.
concepts.work: Goodwill compensation paid by the continuing partners is a real cost to each of them. If the gaining ratio is wrong, one partner pays for a share he never received.

concepts.title: Revaluation on retirement
body: Assets and liabilities are revalued exactly as on admission, through a Revaluation (Profit and Loss Adjustment) Account.
The profit or loss belongs to ALL the existing partners, including the one who is retiring, in the OLD ratio — he was an owner while the values changed.

If the continuing partners do not want the revised values in their balance sheet, they simply compensate the retiring partner: debit the continuing partners in their gaining ratio and credit the retiring partner with his share of the net gain (reverse for a loss). Alternatively a Memorandum Revaluation Account can be used.
concepts.analogy: If the flat you shared went up in value while you lived there, you are entitled to your share of the rise when you move out.
concepts.work: Valuations on retirement are frequently disputed. A clear revaluation account with the valuer's report attached usually settles the argument.

concepts.title: Reserves and accumulated profits
body: Undistributed profits and reserves shown in the balance sheet are credited to ALL partners in the OLD ratio (accumulated losses debited the same way).
Short-cut: if the continuing partners keep their old ratio between themselves, crediting only the retiring partner with his share gives the same result.
If the continuing partners change their mutual ratio and still want the reserve kept in the books, the retiring partner's share is debited to them in the gaining ratio and credited to him.
concepts.analogy: The common savings jar is split by everyone's share before one person leaves — or the stayers buy out the leaver's part of the jar.
concepts.work: A reviewer checks whether the "only the retiring partner's share" short-cut was used where the continuing partners changed ratio — that would be a mistake.

concepts.title: Final amount due and how it is paid
body: Retiring partner's claim = capital (and current account) balance + share of reserves + share of revaluation profit + share of goodwill + share of joint life policy + interest on capital and salary up to the date, if allowed − drawings, interest on drawings and share of losses.

Settlement options: paid in full at once (debit his capital, credit Bank); partly paid and the rest transferred to his Loan A/c; paid in instalments with interest on the outstanding balance; kept as a loan carrying interest or a share of profit; or an annuity for life or a fixed period.

Goodwill (AS 26 — only purchased goodwill may be shown): the retiring partner's share is debited to the gaining partners in the gaining ratio and credited to him. Any goodwill already in the books is first written off among all partners in the old ratio.
concepts.analogy: A final pay-slip: basic dues plus every allowance owed, minus every advance taken.
concepts.work: Banks ask for the retirement deed and the settlement statement before releasing a retiring partner from guarantees — the figures must reconcile with the books.

concepts.title: Paying the retiring partner's loan in instalments
body: When the balance is to be repaid in equal instalments with interest on the outstanding amount, divide the loan by the number of instalments to get the principal part. Each payment = principal instalment + interest on the opening balance of that period.
The loan account is credited with the opening balance (from the capital account) and with interest each year; it is debited with each payment. Interest is a charge against profit of the firm.

blocks.text: Example: ₹60,000 repayable in 3 equal yearly instalments with 10% interest — Year 1 pay 20,000 + 6,000 = ₹26,000; Year 2 pay 20,000 + 4,000 = ₹24,000; Year 3 pay 20,000 + 2,000 = ₹22,000.

concepts.analogy: Like an education loan with equal principal repayments: the interest part shrinks each year because the balance shrinks.
concepts.work: Accountants prepare this schedule at retirement so the firm can plan its cash flow; the interest also has to be reported correctly in the firm's income-tax computation.

concepts.title: Joint Life Policy (JLP)
body: A JLP is taken by the firm on the lives of all partners jointly; the firm pays the premium, and the sum assured is received on the first death or on maturity. It provides cash to pay out a deceased or retiring partner without draining the business.

Three ways of treating the premium: (1) as an expense charged to P&L every year — the policy does not appear in the books; (2) as an asset — debited to Joint Life Policy A/c and written down each year to its surrender value; (3) as an asset with a Joint Life Policy Reserve built up from profits, both shown at surrender value.

On retirement the policy is not received; the retiring partner gets his share of its surrender value. If it is not in the books, it is brought in at surrender value and credited to all partners in the old ratio; if it is shown at a lower figure, only the excess is credited; under the reserve method the reserve is distributed in the old ratio.
concepts.analogy: A savings-cum-insurance pot the firm keeps for the day a partner leaves; when someone leaves early, he gets his slice of what the pot is worth today, not its maturity value.
concepts.work: Auditors confirm the surrender value from the insurer's statement before accepting the retirement settlement.

concepts.title: Separate life policies
body: Instead of one joint policy, the firm may take a separate policy on each partner's life and pay all premiums.
On retirement, the retiring partner is entitled to his profit-sharing proportion of the surrender value of ALL the policies — not just the policy on his own life.
concepts.analogy: Three umbrellas bought from the common purse: the one who leaves gets his share of the value of all three, not merely the one with his name on it.
concepts.work: The settlement working must list every policy with its surrender value certificate; missing one changes the retiring partner's claim.

jobs.title: Settlement statement for a retiring partner
jobs.role: Senior accountant of a trading firm
jobs.situation: A partner holding a 30% share is retiring after 20 years. He has asked for a written statement of everything due to him, and his lawyer will review it.
steps: Confirm from the deed or agreement: valuation of goodwill, interest on capital up to retirement, and how the balance will be paid.
Close the books (or prepare accounts) up to the retirement date so that profit to that date is known.
Prepare the revaluation account with valuer's and insurer's certificates.
List his capital, current account, reserves share, revaluation share, goodwill share and JLP share; deduct drawings.
Draw up the repayment schedule if the balance is a loan in instalments, and record the entries.
jobs.takeaway: Every number in a retirement settlement must be traceable to the deed, the books or a third-party certificate.
jobs.think: The continuing partners say the general reserve should stay in the books. The retiring partner objects. What do you do?
jobs.answer: The reserve can stay in the books, but the retiring partner must still be credited with his share — the continuing partners are debited in their gaining ratio.

jobs.title: Planning cash for an outgoing partner
jobs.role: Finance manager of a partnership firm
jobs.situation: The firm has to pay ₹40 lakh to a retiring partner but has only ₹8 lakh spare cash.
steps: Propose part payment now and the balance as a loan in equal instalments with interest, as allowed by the deed.
Prepare a schedule showing principal, interest and total payment each year; test it against projected cash flows.
Check the surrender value of the joint life policy — sometimes it is cheaper to borrow against it than to raise a bank loan.
jobs.takeaway: Retirement accounting decides how much is owed; the instalment schedule decides whether the firm can survive paying it.

mcqs.q: A, B and C share profits 3:2:1. B retires and nothing is agreed about the future ratio. The new ratio of A and C is:
mcqs.explain: If nothing is agreed about the future ratio, the continuing partners share in their old ratio between themselves. Strike out B's share: A and C continue as 3 : 1. The trap 1 : 1 assumes equal sharing, which applies only when there is no agreement at all on profit sharing — here the old 3 : 2 : 1 agreement still governs A and C. In practice: firms update the deed on a partner's retirement, but if they don't, the old relative ratio carries on.

mcqs.q: X, Y and Z share 2:2:1. Y retires; X and Z will share 3:2. The gaining ratio of X and Z is:
mcqs.explain: Gain = new share − old share. X: 3/5 − 2/5 = 1/5. Z: 2/5 − 1/5 = 1/5. Gaining ratio = 1 : 1. The trap 3 : 2 takes the new ratio as the gaining ratio; they are equal only when continuing partners gain in their old proportion. In practice: the gaining ratio decides how much each continuing partner pays the retiring partner for goodwill, so it is worked out separately.

mcqs.q: Profit on revaluation at the time of retirement is shared by:
options: All partners including the retiring partner, in the old ratio
Continuing partners in the new ratio
Continuing partners in the gaining ratio
The retiring partner alone
mcqs.explain: The changes in asset and liability values occurred while the retiring partner was still an owner, so revaluation profit is shared by all partners, including him, in the old ratio. The trap 'continuing partners in the new ratio' would deny the retiring partner his share of gains made during his time. In practice: when a partner retires from a trading firm, the firm's property is usually revalued so that his settlement reflects current market values.
mcqs.topic: Revaluation of Assets and Liabilities on Retirement of a Partner

mcqs.q: The retiring partner's share of goodwill is debited to:
options: Continuing partners in the gaining ratio
All partners in the old ratio
Goodwill Account
Continuing partners in the new ratio
mcqs.explain: The continuing partners gain the retiring partner's share of future profits, so they compensate him for goodwill in their gaining ratio: debit continuing partners' capitals, credit the retiring partner's capital. The trap is debiting Goodwill Account — raising self-generated goodwill is not allowed under AS 26. In practice: a retiring partner's goodwill share is often the largest component of his final settlement in professional firms.
mcqs.topic: Final Payment to a Retiring Partner

mcqs.q: A loan of ₹90,000 is repayable in 3 equal annual instalments with 10% interest on the balance. The payment at the end of year 2 is:
mcqs.explain: Principal instalment = 90,000 ÷ 3 = ₹30,000 a year. At the end of year 2, the balance outstanding during that year was 90,000 − 30,000 = ₹60,000, so interest = 60,000 × 10% = ₹6,000. Payment = 30,000 + 6,000 = ₹36,000. The trap ₹39,000 is year 1's payment (interest on the full ₹90,000). In practice: firms often settle a retiring partner in instalments with interest to protect their working capital.
mcqs.topic: Paying a Partner’s Loan in Instalment

mcqs.q: A, B and C share 5:3:2. Reserve ₹50,000. C retires and A and B continue in 5:3. Using the short-cut, the entry for the reserve is:
options: Reserve A/c Dr ₹10,000 To C's Capital A/c
Reserve A/c Dr ₹50,000 To A and B in 5:3
C's Capital A/c Dr ₹10,000 To Reserve A/c
No entry
mcqs.explain: Because A and B continue in their old mutual ratio 5 : 3, the short-cut credits only the retiring partner's share of the reserve: 50,000 × 2/10 = ₹10,000. Entry: Reserve A/c Dr ₹10,000, To C's Capital A/c. The trap is distributing the entire reserve, which gives the same result but is not the short-cut asked for; debiting C is simply wrong. In practice: accountants use this short-cut to keep the reserve in the books while settling only the leaver.

mcqs.q: A firm has separate life policies on its three partners (equal partners) with surrender values ₹18,000, ₹24,000 and ₹30,000. The partner whose policy has a surrender value of ₹18,000 retires. His share is:
mcqs.explain: Separate life policies on partners are assets of the firm, so the retiring partner is entitled to his profit-sharing share of the total surrender value of all policies, not just the value of his own policy. Total = 18,000 + 24,000 + 30,000 = ₹72,000; his 1/3 = ₹24,000. The trap ₹18,000 gives him only his own policy's value. In practice: firms often buy separate partner policies to fund settlements on death or retirement.

mcqs.q: Under the method where JLP premium is charged to Profit and Loss Account every year, the joint life policy:
options: Does not appear in the balance sheet
Appears at the sum assured
Appears at the total premium paid
Appears with an equal reserve
mcqs.explain: If JLP premiums are charged to Profit and Loss every year, they are fully written off as expenses, so the policy does not appear as an asset in the balance sheet. On retirement, its surrender value is brought into the books. The trap 'appears at the total premium paid' describes the method where premiums are capitalised. In practice: many small firms expense the premium, so the policy's value appears only when a partner leaves.

mcqs.q: JLP is shown in the books at ₹40,000; its surrender value on a partner's retirement is ₹46,000. The amount credited to the Revaluation Account is:
mcqs.explain: The JLP is already carried at ₹40,000. On retirement it is revalued to its surrender value of ₹46,000, so only the increase of 46,000 − 40,000 = ₹6,000 is a gain credited to the Revaluation Account. The trap ₹46,000 credits the whole surrender value, double-counting the ₹40,000 already in the books. In practice: insurers issue a surrender-value certificate that the firm's accountant uses for this adjustment.

mcqs.q: P, Q and R share 4:3:2. Q retires; P takes 2/9 and R takes 1/9 of the firm's profit from Q's share. The new ratio of P and R is:
mcqs.explain: New share = old share + share taken from Q. P: 4/9 + 2/9 = 6/9. R: 2/9 + 1/9 = 3/9. New ratio = 6 : 3 = 2 : 1. The trap 4 : 3 or 5 : 4 comes from not adding the acquired fractions properly to the old shares. In practice: the deed of retirement records exactly how the retiring partner's share is divided, and the accountant converts it into new ratios.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT credited to a retiring partner's capital account?
options: His drawings during the year
His share of revaluation profit
His share of goodwill
His share of general reserve
mcqs.explain: A retiring partner's capital is credited with everything owed to him: his share of revaluation profit, goodwill, reserves and current-year profit. His drawings during the year reduce what is due, so they are debited, not credited. The trap is goodwill — it is credited because the continuing partners compensate him for it. In practice: the final settlement statement prepared by the firm's CA lists credits and debits so the leaver can verify the amount.
mcqs.topic: Final Payment to a Retiring Partner

mcqs.q: If the continuing partners do not want revised values in their balance sheet, a revaluation gain of ₹30,000 on A's retirement from the firm of A, B and C (equal partners; B and C continue equally) is recorded as:
options: B's Capital Dr ₹5,000, C's Capital Dr ₹5,000 To A's Capital ₹10,000
Revaluation Dr ₹30,000 To A, B, C ₹10,000 each
A's Capital Dr ₹10,000 To B and C
No entry is required
mcqs.explain: Without changing book values, A's share of the revaluation gain (30,000 × 1/3 = ₹10,000) is paid to him by the gainers. B and C each go from 1/3 to 1/2, gaining 1/6 each, so the gaining ratio is 1 : 1. Entry: B's Capital Dr ₹5,000, C's Capital Dr ₹5,000, To A's Capital ₹10,000. The trap is crediting everyone through a Revaluation Account, which changes book values. In practice: this keeps assets at historical cost while settling the leaver fairly.
mcqs.topic: Revaluation of Assets and Liabilities on Retirement of a Partner

questions.q: Pari, Qadir and Rhea share profits 3:2:1. Qadir retires; Pari and Rhea will share future profits 3:2. The balance sheet shows a General Reserve of ₹36,000. The goodwill of the firm is valued at ₹90,000 and is not to appear in the books. (a) Calculate the gaining ratio. (b) Pass the entry for the reserve (i) if it is to be distributed, and (ii) if the continuing partners want it to remain in the books. (c) Pass the entry for goodwill.

model.text: Entries (i) and (ii) are alternatives. The short-cut of crediting only Qadir would be wrong if Pari and Rhea were not debited, because their mutual ratio changes from 3:1 to 3:2.

Part (b)(ii) is answered poorly; many simply write "no entry".

Raising goodwill in the books contrary to the question.

It is to be repaid in three equal annual instalments of principal together with interest at 12% p.a. on the outstanding balance. Prepare Ravi's Loan Account for the three years.

questions.q: Explain the three methods of accounting for the premium on a joint life policy and the treatment on the retirement of a partner.

items: Premium as expense: premium debited to Joint Life Policy Premium A/c and closed to P&L every year; the policy is not in the books. On retirement the surrender value is brought in and credited to all partners in the old ratio.

Premium as asset at surrender value: premium debited to Joint Life Policy A/c; at year-end the excess over surrender value is written off to P&L. On retirement only any increase in surrender value over book value is a gain.

Joint Life Policy Reserve: as in the second method, plus an amount equal to the premium is set aside from profits to a JLP Reserve, which is brought down to the surrender value; both appear at surrender value. On retirement the reserve is distributed in the old ratio.
In all methods the retiring partner receives his share of the surrender value; the policy continues for the others.

scheme.pt: Expense method and its retirement treatment
Asset (surrender value) method and its treatment
Retiring partner gets share of surrender value, not policy amount

remarks: Answers often confuse surrender value with sum assured — on retirement the policy has not matured.
mistakes: Saying the retiring partner gets his share of the policy amount.
tips: Number the three methods and give the entry in brief for each.

summary: Gain = new share − old share; nothing agreed → continuing partners keep their old ratio (gaining ratio = old ratio).
Revaluation profit/loss → all partners incl. retiring partner, old ratio.
Reserves → all partners, old ratio (short-cut: only the retiring partner, if continuing partners keep their mutual ratio).
Goodwill → retiring partner credited; gaining partners debited in gaining ratio.
Claim settled in cash, as a loan, in instalments with interest or as an annuity.
JLP: expense / asset at surrender value / reserve method; retiring partner gets share of surrender value. Separate policies: share of surrender value of all policies.
remember: Instalment payment = principal instalment + interest on opening balance.
Only the excess of surrender value over book value is a revaluation gain.
The retiring partner's capital account must close at nil.
traps: Don't use the new ratio for goodwill — use the gaining ratio.
Don't use the short-cut for reserves when the continuing partners change their mutual ratio.
Don't give the retiring partner the sum assured of a JLP — he gets the surrender value share.

viva.q: What is gaining ratio and how is it calculated on the retirement of a partner?
viva.model: Gaining ratio is the ratio in which the continuing partners acquire the retiring partner's share. Each partner's gain is his new share minus his old share. If no new ratio is agreed, the continuing partners keep their old ratio and the gaining ratio is the same as their old ratio. It is used to debit them with the retiring partner's share of goodwill.

viva.q: In what ratio is profit on revaluation shared when a partner retires, and why?
viva.model: Profit or loss on revaluation is shared by all the partners, including the retiring partner, in the old profit sharing ratio, because the values changed while the retiring partner was still a partner.

viva.q: What items are added to or deducted from a retiring partner's capital to find the amount payable to him?
viva.model: To his capital we add his share of reserves and undistributed profits, his share of revaluation profit, his share of goodwill, his share of the joint life policy, and interest on capital or salary if allowed up to the date of retirement. We deduct his drawings, interest on drawings and his share of any losses or revaluation loss. The balance is paid to him or transferred to his loan account.

viva.q: How is a general reserve treated on retirement if the continuing partners do not change their mutual ratio?
viva.model: Normally the reserve is distributed among all partners in the old ratio. But if the continuing partners keep their old ratio between themselves, it is enough to credit only the retiring partner's capital with his share of the reserve, because the gaining ratio is the same as their old ratio and the result is identical.

viva.q: What are the three methods of treating joint life policy premium?
viva.model: First, the premium can be treated as an expense and charged to profit and loss account every year, so the policy does not appear in the books. Second, it can be treated as an asset and the policy is shown at its surrender value, the excess premium being written off. Third, a joint life policy reserve is created out of profits, and both the policy and the reserve appear at the surrender value.

cases.title: Uma retires from Tanvi, Uma & Varun
cases.case: Tanvi, Uma and Varun share profits 5:3:2. Uma retires; Tanvi and Varun will share 3:2. Uma's capital is ₹1,50,000 and the General Reserve is ₹20,000. The goodwill of the firm is valued at ₹1,00,000 and will not appear in the books. The firm has a joint life policy whose premiums have always been charged to Profit and Loss Account; its surrender value is ₹40,000. There is no revaluation.

mcqs.q: What is the gaining ratio of Tanvi and Varun?
mcqs.explain: Gain = new share − old share. Tanvi: 3/5 − 5/10 = 6/10 − 5/10 = 1/10. Varun: 2/5 − 2/10 = 4/10 − 2/10 = 2/10. Gaining ratio = 1 : 2. The trap 3 : 2 is the new ratio, not the gain; Varun actually gains twice as much as Tanvi. In practice: Uma's goodwill will be paid by Tanvi and Varun in this 1 : 2 gaining ratio.

mcqs.q: How much is debited to Varun's capital for Uma's goodwill?
mcqs.explain: Uma's share of goodwill = 1,00,000 × 3/10 = ₹30,000. Tanvi and Varun pay it in their gaining ratio 1 : 2, so Varun is debited 30,000 × 2/3 = ₹20,000 and Tanvi ₹10,000. The trap ₹12,000 uses the new ratio 3 : 2 (Varun 2/5), and ₹10,000 is Tanvi's part. In practice: goodwill compensation is passed through capital accounts so no goodwill asset appears in the books.
mcqs.topic: Final Payment to a Retiring Partner

mcqs.q: What is Uma's share of the joint life policy?
mcqs.explain: Since premiums were charged to profit and loss, the JLP is not in the books; its surrender value of ₹40,000 is brought in on retirement. Uma's share in the old ratio = 40,000 × 3/10 = ₹12,000. The trap ₹40,000 gives her the whole surrender value — the policy is not paid out on retirement, only on maturity or death. In practice: insurers provide a surrender-value certificate, and the firm records it before settling the retiring partner.

mcqs.q: What is the total amount due to Uma?
mcqs.explain: Amount due = capital 1,50,000 + reserve share 20,000 × 3/10 = 6,000 + goodwill share 30,000 + JLP share 12,000 = ₹1,98,000. The trap ₹1,86,000 forgets the JLP; ₹1,92,000 forgets the reserve; ₹1,68,000 forgets goodwill. In practice: a retiring partner's settlement statement lists each component, and the firm may pay part immediately and the rest in instalments with interest.
